title: Honey
full_review:
"Honey" (Universal) is no sweet treat. The superficial music drama follows the story of the title's young hip-hop dancer as she finally gets her big break to not only star in music videos, but also choreograph them.

Honey (played by Jessica Alba of television's "Dark Angel" series) is a 22-year-old from the Bronx who spends her days teaching hip-hop classes to the neighborhood kids at the local community center run by her mother (Lonette McKee). At night she bartends at a happening club where she gets to strut her stuff on the dance floor. But Honey's big dream is to star in music videos. Who would have guessed?

Director Billie Woodruff, who has directed several music videos, makes his feature film debut with "Honey." But the leap to the big screen seems too much for him as the film lacks any get-up-and-go despite energetic dance scenes and a kickin' music score likely to be familiar to kids. The tired rags-to-riches story is held together with Scotch tape. The film feels more like an excuse to show off hair and makeup and the latest skin-tight, skimpy fashions than a sincere effort to tell a compelling story.

Predictably, Honey is discovered by video mogul Michael Ellis (David Moscow), who not only launches Honey's dance career but also catapults her into the world of music video choreography. This threadbare story line offers the film an excuse to fill time with cameo appearances by hip-hop and R&B stars such as Missy Elliott (whose sassiness steals the show), Ginuwine, Tweet, and Shawn Desman, to name a few. Parents should be aware that some of these dance videos have a few racy moves as the dancers bump and grind. But, unfortunately, it's nothing worse than what kids may already be seeing on MTV.

Alba, though likable and certainly attractive, has very little emotional range. But then again, her cardboard character has little to do other than pout, wear the latest hip-hop wear and boogie on the dance floor. Honey, refreshingly, is "not that kind of girl" and her romance with Chaz (Mekhi Phifer, slumming a bit) is thankfully of the innocent kind, with the two kissing and then the film fading to black. And when video mogul Michael tries to make the moves on Honey, his advances are met with a stinging slap in the face.

None of the various subplots penetrates beyond the surface. Honey feels the pull of her urban roots and puts on a benefit concert to raise money to erect a neighborhood dance studio. Lil' Romeo plays a street kid from a broken home with a gift for dancing who is "saved" from the local drug dealer by Honey. And even when Michael has blackballed Honey from the industry, she manages to rise above it and be sought out by none other than Missy Elliott.

However, as banal and mostly innocuous as "Honey" is, there are a few spots that are troubling. At the opening of the film, Honey's girlfriend Gina (Joy Bryant) gropes her own breasts while on the dance floor. It's not quite a dance move, and it certainly is unnecessary. It seems to have been included to earn the film the coveted PG-13 rating that most filmmakers seem to think is attractive to their target audience. The other bothersome aspect is that nearly every character sports a cross on a chain. It is more of a fashion statement than an assertion about a belief system, which reduces the cross' symbolism to something trendy rather than meaningful.

Pass on "Honey."

Because of a few fleeting sexual references, a crude gesture, intermittent crass language and fleeting drug content, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
